title: Power & Energy Fundamentals
summary: Dynamic vs static power, and why voltage — not frequency — is the lever engineers reach for first to cut power.

slides.subTitle: The cost of switching
slides.markdown:
**Dynamic power** is consumed every time a transistor actually switches state, and follows `P_dynamic = C x V^2 x f` — proportional to switched **capacitance** (C, roughly chip size/complexity), the **square** of voltage (V), and **frequency** (f, how often switching happens).

This is the power cost of *doing work* — every clock tick that flips transistors from 0 to 1 or back pays this cost, which is why it scales directly with how fast and how much of the chip is actively switching.

slides.subTitle: Leakage, drawn even at rest
slides.markdown:
**Static (leakage) power** is drawn even when transistors aren't switching at all — tiny currents leak through transistors that are nominally "off" due to their physical construction at very small scales. Unlike dynamic power, it doesn't depend on activity, only on how many transistors exist and how leaky each one is.

As process nodes have shrunk (smaller transistors), leakage has grown from a rounding error into a substantial fraction of total chip power — modern chips can burn meaningful power even sitting idle.

slides.subTitle: The quadratic term
slides.markdown:
Because dynamic power scales with **V-squared** but only **linearly** with frequency, cutting voltage is the single biggest lever for reducing power: halving voltage cuts dynamic power to a quarter, while halving frequency only cuts it in half.

The catch is that lower voltage also slows down how fast transistors can switch reliably, capping how low voltage can go before the clock frequency has to drop to compensate — which is exactly the trade-off DVFS (a later topic) manages at runtime.

slides.subTitle: Dynamic vs static power over time
slides.markdown:
As transistors have shrunk across process generations, the balance between the two power sources has shifted.

![A rough dynamic-vs-static power breakdown across process generations](assets/dynamic-static-power-trend.svg)

Older, larger nodes were almost entirely dynamic-dominated; leakage was negligible. Modern, smaller nodes see static power claim a far larger share — why chip design now actively fights leakage, not just switching.

slides.subTitle: Instantaneous vs integrated
slides.markdown:
**Power** is instantaneous draw (watts, at this moment). **Energy** is power integrated over time (joules — how much total was consumed over a task). A chip can have high power but low energy if it finishes fast; a chip with lower power but a much longer runtime can consume more total energy for the same task.

This is why "finish faster" isn't automatically "greener" — a design must be judged on energy-per-task (often stated as energy-to-solution) for a fair comparison, not on peak power draw alone.

slides.subTitle: Frequency vs voltage vs capacitance
slides.markdown:
| Lever | Power effect | Performance cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reduce frequency | Linear power reduction | Direct, proportional slowdown | Simple, but a poor power-per-performance trade alone |
| Reduce voltage | Quadratic power reduction | Requires a frequency cut too, past a point | Best power-per-performance trade — the primary lever |
| Reduce switched capacitance | Linear power reduction | Requires design/architecture changes (smaller structures, clock gating) | Effective but harder to change at runtime |

**How to decide:** voltage's quadratic effect makes it the first lever engineers reach for — DVFS exploits exactly this by lowering voltage and frequency together during low-demand periods, buying large power savings for a comparatively small performance cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: what a voltage cut really buys
slides.subTitle: Quadratic vs linear, side by side
slides.markdown:
Baseline: V = 1.0V, f = 3.0GHz, dynamic power = 10W (some fixed C absorbed into the constant).

```
halve frequency only (f=1.5GHz, V unchanged):
  power ratio = f_new/f_old = 0.5 -> power = 5W (50% cut)
  performance: roughly halved

halve voltage only (V=0.5V, f unchanged) -- often not achievable in practice,
but illustrating the pure V^2 term:
  power ratio = (V_new/V_old)^2 = 0.25 -> power = 2.5W (75% cut)
  performance: unchanged (frequency didn't move)

realistic DVFS step (both drop together, V=0.8V, f=2.4GHz):
  power ratio = (0.8)^2 * 0.8 = 0.512 -> power ~= 5.1W (49% cut)
  performance: ~20% slower (f dropped 20%)
```

The realistic combined step gets close to the frequency-only power cut but for far less performance loss, because voltage's quadratic term is doing most of the work — which is exactly why DVFS always drops voltage alongside frequency rather than touching either alone.

slides.subTitle: Sometimes running faster saves more energy than running slower
slides.markdown:
Naive intuition says lower power always means lower energy — but energy is power *times time*, and a chip that finishes a burst of work faster can enter a deep, extremely low-power **sleep state** sooner. "**Race-to-sleep**" is the strategy of running at high frequency (higher instantaneous power) specifically to finish quickly and spend more total time in an idle low-power state, rather than running slowly the whole time at moderate power.

This is why mobile SoCs don't simply run at the lowest sustainable clock speed for battery life — for bursty, intermittent workloads (checking notifications, a brief UI animation), racing to finish and sleeping deeply often wins on total energy consumed versus plodding through at low power with the chip staying "awake" (and leaking static power, [Static Power](power-and-energy-fundamentals)) for far longer.

slides.sectionTitle: TDP: a real number with a specific meaning
slides.subTitle: What a spec sheet's power number actually promises
slides.markdown:
**TDP (thermal design power)** is the sustained heat output a chip's cooling solution is designed to dissipate — not the chip's absolute peak power draw, and not its typical average draw either. It's a **cooling-system design target**: a laptop or server vendor picks a heatsink/fan rated for the TDP figure, and the chip's firmware is allowed to boost well above TDP briefly (a burst) as long as thermal sensors keep it from sustaining that level indefinitely.

This is why two chips with the "same TDP" can behave very differently under sustained load — TDP says nothing about how long a boost clock lasts, only what the steady-state thermal budget is. A chip that boosts aggressively for 10 seconds then throttles hard to stay near its TDP will benchmark very differently on a short burst test versus a long sustained-load test, even though both report the identical TDP number.
